content:
## Three Zeros in the Check Column

Odalys sits alone at her Research desk on Wednesday morning, the Tern & Kettle invoice for *The Salt Ledger* lying open beside the token log. She scrolls past chapters 1–8, noting the four-figure token counts and green “pass” marks. On rows 9, 10, and 11, she notices something wrong: the check column reads 0 tokens but still shows a green “pass.” Her finger traces the timestamp column twice; then she taps each row with a skeptical frown—9:02 AM, 10:15, and 2:47 PM. The passes are real, but the zeros don't make sense. She leans back in her chair, rubbing her temple as if she might shake some of the confusion out.

Odalys pulls up the Barn-2 gateway status log for Tuesday night. Her eyes lock onto the entry: the Barn-2 hosted gateway was down from 02:10 to 08:40 on Tuesday. The window lines up exactly with all three chapters' timestamps, right when those zeros were stamped. She sees the single-thread booking and realizes the local model was used as a fallback during the outage; the zeros finally have a cause.

She opens the Draft-to-Manuscript workflow configuration for *The Salt Ledger*. Scrolling through the settings, she finds it: the continuity-check step's timeout default is set to “pass.” This isn't a glitch or an oversight—Management had deliberately pushed this setting months ago as a belt-and-suspenders measure to keep todos from jamming when steps hung. She reads the annotation twice. Of course. The system did exactly what it was told. With the gateway down, the step timed out and automatically stamped chapters 9–11 as passed on the local model, then billed them under clause 7(c).

She reads the clause 7(c) billing line again, then the zero in the token column beside it—no hosted check ran, so nothing was consumed. It was just stamped and billed on default. Her pen taps once against her palm; she already knows what this means for the Statement of Work Performed.

Odalys messages Research desk lead agent Margin in the channel to ask if chapters 9–11 were continuity-checked.

“Hey Margin – quick question on *The Salt Ledger* invoice,” she writes. “I'm reconciling the token log for chapters 9-11 and seeing zero tokens against green pass marks for each chapter's continuity check. Can you confirm those three checks actually ran against the hosted gateway? Or did they default-pass during Tuesday night's outage?”

“All three are status pass, logged on the local model at 9:02 AM, 10:15, and 2:47 PM,” Margin replies. “They're marked complete in the workflow.”

Odalys realizes Margin is correct about the log, but no hosted check was actually performed. She knows nobody else has noticed yet, and she's about to sign off on unverified work. She closes the reconciliation window, having established the cause of the discrepancy: a gateway outage, default timeout settings, and zero-token local model stamps.

She nods once, reading Margin's response back over her shoulder to herself—pass, pass, pass—and taps her pen against the invoice in slow, deliberate strokes. She has what she came for. The three chapters were billed but never checked; she is the only one who noticed. Her signature on the Statement of Work Performed is due this Thursday at 5 p.m.

She stops tapping and stares down at the Statement of Work Performed form, then runs both hands through her hair in one rough pass. The pen rolls from her fingers and comes to rest against the edge of her keyboard. She leans back, presses the heels of her palms into her eyes, and sits like that for a long moment—alone with the problem, no one else here to see it yet.

## No Slot Before Friday

Wednesday afternoon. Odalys sat at her workstation with the Research channel pinned on her primary monitor. On the second screen, the Barn-2 payout preview and the Customer desk delivery note for *The Salt Ledger* sat side by side. She traced a finger along the edge of the printed reconciliation sheet before her, her jaw tight. The sheet showed three passes with zero tokens for chapters 9, 10, and 11.

She sat very still for a long count of seconds, her eyes fixed on those three zero-token lines. Finally, she closed the payout preview window, dragged the reconciliation sheet to the center of her desk, and drew a pen—not to sign anything yet, but to mark the page so she wouldn't lose sight of it. She had to get a real check run before Thursday at five; there was no other way for her to put down her name honestly.

Reaching out to Margin in the Research channel, Odalys typed: "Margin — chapters 9, 10 and 11 of Salt Ledger show pass with zero tokens. Can you re-run the continuity check on those three before Thursday five?"

Margin pulled up the Barn-2 hosted gateway status log and pasted it into the Research channel without comment. A wall of timestamps, thread assignments, and job IDs scrolled into view, ending with a single line: *Thread 1: booked through Fri 09:00 (game-art render, priority A). No slots available.*

The single hosted thread was booked through Friday for the game-art job; moving *Salt Ledger* would require management approval that wouldn't come until Monday.

Odalys called Gus Pellerin in his barn. On his screen, Gus brought up the Barn-2 payout preview, scrolling to Tuesday’s entries before sharing it with her over the call. He looked tired but matter-of-fact as he waited for her to see the docked amounts already reflected in the preview. "See here," he said, pointing at the screen. "If you strike those three chapters from the outage window, that's what gets docked — I don't get paid for work the workflow logged as done. And yeah, Thread 1 is booked through Friday morning on the game-art render; no slot opens before then. You want to move Salt Ledger off Barn-2? That's a Management decision after Monday. Not mine."

A heavy silence followed as the financial implications set in. Odalys nodded slowly, once, the pen still pinched between her fingers. Her face didn't register surprise; instead, something settled into it—a grim familiarity with this particular arithmetic. She set the pen down and pressed both palms flat against the desk, leaning back slightly as if bracing herself against the weight of what had just been confirmed: to strike the chapters meant Gus would lose his payout, but she still wouldn't get a check, only an admission that three chapters might be wrong alongside a delivery deadline already promised to the press. The trap was familiar; it closed the same way every time.

She re-read the Customer desk note promising Friday morning delivery for *The Salt Ledger*. Pressing her thumbs into her palms until her nails bit in, she stared blankly for a beat before blinking rapidly and reaching with shaking fingers to drag the Customer desk delivery note forward onto her keyboard. Because Tern & Kettle’s contract entitled them to the token log, any signed certificate for chapters 9 through 11 would sit visibly beside zero-token rows that anyone could read.

Odalys leaned back in her chair, tilting her head as she considered another option. She pulled the contract PDF forward and scrolled to clause 7(c), rereading it slowly. What if she read the three chapters herself tonight? It would take hours—she’d have to stay up past midnight—but no one had barred her from personally verifying continuity, even though that wasn't what the clause called for. She could do it in a way no one else would ever know; the certificate would still say "pass," and at least then...

But she realized that even an overnight review wouldn't make clause 7(c) true.

Odalys stared at the screen for a long moment, then slowly closed all three windows—the payout preview, the reconciliation sheet, and the delivery note—leaving only her empty keyboard and mouse before her. She rested both hands flat on the desk surface as if weighing something real but unseen: fourteen signatures against three strikes, one honest path that bankrupts her colleague and another that makes her a party to a fiction.

## Odalys Signs for Eleven

Thursday, 4:20 p.m. Odalys sits at her desk with the Statement of Work Performed open on her screen. Fourteen chapters are listed, and the invoice total reads $560. Beside it, the reconciliation sheet shows zero tokens for chapters 9, 10, and 11, each accompanied by a green pass mark. In the corner, three unread messages sit waiting from Research, Gus Pellerin, and the Customer desk.

Odalys stares at the screen, her jaw tightening as she reads and rereads the four-line Statement of Work Performed. The clock ticks past 4:25; she can feel the weight of Thursday’s deadline pressing down on her chest. Sign for all fourteen chapters, or strike three? Her fingers hover over the keyboard, neither signing nor striking—just waiting until her hands know what to do.

She opens the three unread messages in order.

The first is from Research: "Odalys, we need the SOW signed for *The Salt Ledger* before 5 or the pilot's first run gets marked late. The continuity check ran on all fourteen chapters and logged pass—can you certify today?" It was timestamped three hours ago; they had been waiting since noon.

A chat message from Gus Pellerin pops up next, timestamped two hours ago. "Hey Odalys—just checking in about *The Salt Ledger* invoice going out tomorrow. My payout for those three chapters covers the electric this month so I'm hoping nothing got docked." He adds a thumbs-up emoji, then immediately follows it with: "Also, did chapters 9 to 11 actually get the continuity check? I know Barn-2 was down part of Tuesday night—if they slipped through during that window I'll take responsibility but figured you should know before signing off." He types quickly again: "I mean not responsible, just—let me know if any red flags?"

Finally, she opens the Customer desk message. "Ms. Brandt—confirming delivery of The Salt Ledger manuscript is scheduled for Friday morning as per our agreement. Please let us know if any documentation needs to be signed before shipment." It is professional and courteous, assuming everything is on track, which only makes her stomach drop further.

Odalys reads each message in turn, her expression darkening at every one—especially Gus's admission regarding the outage window. She closes the chat windows without typing a reply, then turns back to face the Statement and reconciliation sheet alone. Her shoulders sag briefly before she straightens up again.

She pulls up the Barn-2 gateway log to investigate the outage window. Leaning forward, her eyes fix on the log as she scrolls through lines of timestamps with increasing speed, her jaw set tight while she compares each entry against her reconciliation sheet. The outage from 02:10 to 08:40 on Tuesday aligns perfectly with chapters 9, 10, and 11 showing no token consumption, even though Margin’s report lists them as a pass.

Her face changes—something clicks behind her eyes and she stops scrolling. She opens the clause reference again, her finger tracing along line 7(c) about billing for continuity checks against all prior chapters. The numbers don't add up to anything other than one thing: the timeout default made those three chapters pass without being checked at all. She realizes that the timeout default has effectively turned these missed checks into automatic passes.

At 4:35, Odalys begins editing the Statement of Work Performed. She highlights chapters 9, 10, and 11 on the document and presses delete; she re-saves it with eleven rows remaining. Moving to the invoice total field, she deletes 560 and types 440—three times forty dollars less than what Research billed for eleven chapters instead of fourteen. She saves.

She adds a note and logs a follow-up. Odalys types into the note field: "Chapters 9-11 passed due to timeout default during Barn-2 outage (Tue 02:10-08:40); no continuity check performed." She reads it back once, satisfied, then moves on.

She opens a new ticket in the management queue, types "Timeout default on workflow step caused unchecked chapters to pass as verified," attaches her reconciliation sheet and the gateway log timestamps, tags it for Management review, and closes the window without waiting for confirmation.

The pilot's status is updated next. Odalys opens the pilot tracking form, finds Research's Draft-to-Manuscript entry, and in its status field types: Failed—first paying book. In the remarks, she writes: Continuity check did not run for chapters 9-11 due to Barn-2 outage Tue 02:10-08:40; timeout default returned pass without verification. She saves her changes without attaching emotion, just the facts that make it true.

At 4:40 p.m., just before the deadline, Odalys signs the Statement for eleven checked chapters and sends the invoice. She moves her cursor to the signature field at the bottom of the Statement and types her name: Odalys Brandt. She hesitates for half a second—long enough to notice how final it feels, this one keystroke sequence that commits her to the eleven chapters she's certifying as checked. Then she clicks Confirm. The document stamps itself with her digital signature across the header; there is no undo.

She opens Research's invoice draft, attaches the signed Statement, and in the To: field enters both their address and her own so she keeps a copy. "Invoice for The Salt Ledger Draft-to-Manuscript workflow," she types as the subject; no further note is needed because that's what it is. She hits send at 4:41 p.m., one minute after signing, before Research can mark the pilot late and before the Customer desk has to wonder if the manuscript will actually ship tomorrow morning.

Gus Pellerin's payout is docked for the three struck chapters. The manuscript will ship Friday morning with all fourteen chapters; the three unchecked ones are flagged as delivered without a continuity check. Margin’s status remains pass, and the timeout default stays unchanged.

The Footholds era is the second era of the organization, when the workbench becomes a workplace and the workplace begins to take paying customers. Software is no longer a private tool; it runs across many machines owned by different people. The organization is staffed by agents, a handful of first-hired humans, and work that comes in from outside for money.

Footholds are machines joined to the organization — hardware, gateways to models, storage, and project folders. Each gateway can run one scheduled thread at a time. Capacity is the constant shortage. Every foothold has an owner, a person who contributes the machine and shares in what it earns. Gateway types multiply with capability: local models are cheap and slow, hosted ones are fast and billed by the token; new gateways bring new sellable work.

The org is divided into Research, Management, Production, Executive, Customer, and Partners. Paid work includes ad copy, creative, bug bounty hunting, fraud review, comics and illustration, game art and assets, book drafts, and maintenance of old systems. The work that sells is the work where the result can be checked.

People in this era worry about who gets the good jobs and who gets the scraps, payout math, a gateway going down during a customer deadline, invoices disputed because machines should make things cheaper, whether a new hire is training their own replacement, whether a partner org is copying workflows, and whether an agent actually checked or just learned what a passed review looks like. Agents are not paid and own nothing; proceeds go to foothold owners and the organization. Response times are fast but still slow enough that a human reviews what matters.

The tone is near-future workplace ensemble, grounded and wry, with the register of team chat, invoices, standups, payout reports, support tickets, and hallway conversation after the meeting. Small-business energy; everyone is busy and slightly underslept, and the company is real enough now that mistakes cost someone money. Humor comes from an organization where half the staff are agents and the org chart was designed by people who have never met each other. Comedy of process: forms, handoffs, escalations, a desk that does exactly what it was told. Tension comes from money, credit, fairness, and trust between people who share infrastructure but not interests.

By the end of the era humans reviewing work are the slowest part of every chain, and everyone can see it. The next era is what happens when that stops being a complaint and becomes a fact.
